To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the CAG expanded repeat number is the major determinant of juvenile age of onset; (2) the gender effect of affected parent is weaker in juvenile than in adult HD; (3) the TAA‐triple in GluR 6 is a major determinant of juvenile HD age at onset.

(i) the mean parent–offspring CAG repeat change is larger in paternal vs. in maternal meiotic transmissions; (ii) the mean parent‐offspring year‐of‐age change is similar in the two meiotic transmissions; and (iii) the age‐of‐on‐set is earlier in juvenile patients with lower TAA‐repeat number in GluR‐6 gene.

the gender effect of parent on age at juvenile HD onset is weaker in Italian patients than in other populations, and that the effect is amplified by other genetic features, such as the GluR 6 polymorphism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the gender effect in juvenile HD patients of Italian origin, and the role of the CAG repeat number and the TAA triplet length in the Glur6 gene.
the study of a population of patients affected by juvenile Huntington disease (juvenile HD) of Italian origin.
the study of the genetic and environmental factors involved in the onset and progression of HD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the CAG expansion in the paternal transmission is associated with an earlier HD onset and a more severe phenotype, but this effect is not as strong as the effect of CAG repeat length on HD age at onset and severity.
, in the Italian juvenile HD population studied, the gender effect on age at disease onset is weaker than in the adult population.
the gender of the affected parent does not affect juvenile HD age at onset, although the CAG repeat number in the paternal vs. maternal transmission is longer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CAG mutation length in the HD gene is longer in paternallly transmitted HD juvenile subjects of Italian origin than in maternallly transmitted juvenile HD subjects.

the gender effect on age at disease onset and CAG repeat length is more pronounced in adult HD patients than in juvenile patients, and that the GluR gene polymorphism is a relevant modifier of the juvenile HD phenotype.
the gender effect of CAG repeat expansion is not a simple phenomenon, but it is modulated by genetic factors, which may differ according to the population under investigation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gender effect of HD is different for juvenile and for adult patients, and that this is possibly amplified by other factors, such as genetic ones.
the gender effect on age at HD onset is not as evident in juvenile as in adult HD patients.
the gender effect of HD in Italian families is different from the gender effect in other populations.
